subject: Suggestion for prior distribution of slope parameter when having a specific hypothesis on its value

messages.author: 1cdecf6324f43598
messages.subject: Suggestion for prior distribution of slope parameter when having a specific hypothesis on its value
parts:
Dear all,

First of I love stan it has really made life so much easier. Great thing and its only been getting better and better.

So to my question:

I have a model with the following structure:

y = a*x^b

and fit it on log-log coordinates:

log(y) = b*log(x) + a

Due to a very strong theory we are developing we have excellent reason to believe that the slope, b, should take on a value of exactly 3/2 based on first principles.

How would you reason from a Bayesian perspective on what prior to use to evaluate this hypothesis?

Any suggestions or pointers to literature are much appreciated.

Regards,
Daniel Fürth

PhD student
Department of Neuroscience
Karolinska Institutet
Stockholm Sweden

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Suggestion for prior distribution of slope parameter when having a specific hypothesis on its value
parts:
I don't understand what you mean by "first principles", because
if first principles say a value has to be 1.5, then you should just
set it to 1.5.

If I understand your literal question, namely test the hypothesis
that theta = 1.5, then the answer is 0 for a Bayesian, because

Pr[theta = 1.5 | data] = 0

unless the prior or likelihood prohibit values other than 1.5.

You could estimate

Pr[(1.5 - epsilon) < theta < (1.5 + epsilon) | data],

which should always be positive assuming the posterior has support
in an interval around theta.

The joy of Bayesian inference is that if the data constrains
theta to be very close to 1.5, then posterior inference will
take that into account without your having to make a hard
hypothesis-test type decision.

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Suggestion for prior distribution of slope parameter when having a specific hypothesis on its value
parts:
Hi, I think the point is that when you have a parameter with a true value of 1.5 (say) in the theoretical model, it won’t be exactly 1.5 when fit to data, because of measurement error and misspecification. In your setting, one option is to just set b to 1.5 as data and then check the fit of your model using posterior predictive checks.
Another option is to give b a fairly strong prior, such as N(1.5, .5) which will pull the estimate toward your prior model. Yet another approach is to set b to 1.5 and then add another parameter to capture model misspecification.
